targetedCascade.correction: 0x021144CC was recorded as a target selector by Stage 4 B08 and by this file's first edition. It is not. It is a first-fit affordability scan over the group list at combatant + 0xE8 + group*12 (count byte at + 0xF0 + group*12), returning the first action id whose ARM9 0x020CFF9C record (stride 104) has +0x48 strictly below the reserve, else 0. Order matters; there is no shuffle.
targetedCascade.realTargetChoice: Inlined at 0x02115BE8. Walks the roster at combatant +0x54, skipping a null entry or one whose HP is exactly 0, and keeps the entry with the greatest parallel metric at roster +0x44 + index*4. movgt means ties keep the earlier entry; the running best starts at 0 so a metric of 0 or less never wins.
targetedCascade.hpAsymmetry: This scan skips HP == 0 but accepts negative HP, unlike battleContactTargeting which requires HP > 0. The asymmetry is in the ROM and is preserved.
targetedCascade.cascadeOrder: Six groups in the order 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, then the move ladder. Group 2 is guarded by [[+0x54]+0x40] > 0 and targets SELF with no roster scan. Group 1 needs an affordable action plus a metric44 roster target. Group 4 is guarded by [[+0x54]+0x50] > 0 and targets SELF. Group 3 targets the greatest metric54. Group 6 targets SELF but declines when the combatant already carries the effect the action would apply. Group 5 collects up to three living entries whose +0x160 is 0 and picks among them uniformly with a second channel-216 roll.
targetedCascade.threeLivenessRules: The cascade applies three different liveness tests. Group 1 skips a null entry or HP exactly 0. Group 3 (0x02115CFC..0x02115D18) applies NO HP test at all, so a defeated entry is a legal target. Group 5 requires HP > 0. All three are in the ROM and are preserved rather than normalised. battleContactTargeting separately requires HP > 0, so a negative-HP combatant can be selected by group 1 or 3 and then rejected at contact.
targetedCascade.duplicateEffectCheck: OVL19 0x021300D4, u32 by action id, maps an action to the positive effect code it would apply: ids 0-9 map to 0, then 10/11 to 1, 12/13 to 2, up to 22/23 to 7. Group 6 declines when combatant +0x160 already equals that code. Because the first ten entries are 0, an action with no effect is always declined by a combatant with no effect. This is the duplicate/active-effect logic Stage 6 observed while auditing Sense.
targetedCascade.tableAdjacencyNote: 0x021300D4 sits 88 bytes past the field matrix base 0x0213007C, exactly where matrix row 8 would begin. The matrix's zero tail and this table's zero head occupy the same bytes, so both readings agree with the ROM and battleDamageResolver's rows 8-10 of zeros remain correct. Do not treat this as a conflict.
targetedCascade.fieldCorrection: +0x64 is the target and +0x178 is the chosen action id; +0x174 holds the pointer built from that id by multiplying by 104. An earlier reading of +0x178 as the target was wrong.
targetedCascade.sixBoundedLoopCount: Corrected 2026-09-01: OVL19 holds 24 six-bounded loops, not 19, and all 24 increment. The conclusion is unchanged and now rests on a mechanical check of every one of them.

items.method: Scanned ARM9 and all 22 overlays for a load of combatant +0x160 followed within four instructions by a compare against an immediate.
items.evidence: Fourteen such sites exist in total. OVL19 compares the positive effect code against 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. It never compares against 4. ARM9, OVL9 and OVL18 only compare against 0, which is a presence test.
items.conclusion: Sense has no value-specific branch anywhere in the ROM's ARM code. Its only mechanical footprint is through != 0 tests: group 6's duplicate decline and group 5's target collection. This matches Stage 6's audit and extends it from OVL19 to the whole image.
items.notImplemented: Nothing to implement. An accuracy or must-hit effect for code 4 would be an invention.

items.method: Enumerated every read of action +0x48 in OVL19 and checked which one writes back.
items.evidence: Five reads: the charge at 0x0211C244, the affordability scan at 0x02114504, the two AI ladder gates at 0x02115AA8 and 0x02115AFC, and 0x0210BDE8 which masks a hardware register at 0x04001008 and is unrelated. Only 0x0211C244 writes: cmp current(stats +0x54) against cost, blt returns 0 without charging, otherwise sub and str back to +0x54.
items.conclusion: A spendable action resource exists. Current is stats +0x54, maximum is stats +0x5C, cost is action +0x48 as a u16. The guard is signed less-than, so paying down to exactly zero is allowed and a refused action costs nothing. This also gives the AI reserve its meaning: min(trunc(max * profilePercent / 100), current).
items.residual: Regeneration, starting value and any writer outside OVL19 are untraced. The module charges and refuses; it does not restore.

items.method: Enumerated every access to the pending reward field +0x408 in OVL8 and located them relative to the mode jump table at 0x0210D1A0.
items.evidence: The reward-decision function writes +0x408 exactly twice, at 0x0210D128 (default 0) and 0x0210D190 (the payout), and both are BEFORE the jump table. None of the three destinations (mode 1 at 0x0210D3EC, mode 2 at 0x0210D1C0, default at 0x0210D464) writes it.
items.conclusion: The payout is locked before any mode branch runs, so there is no first-clear bonus, no rank multiplier and no streak. Mode 2's per-opponent already-cleared flag at +0xC0 gates presentation and progression, not the amount.
items.alsoFound: 0x0210EA48 is not a bonus either: it moves the pending amount into the wallet in steps of 1, 10 or 100 depending on magnitude, which is the counting-up tally. The instant path at 0x0210EAB0 transfers the remainder whole. Neither changes the total.

items.method: Read the per-frame combatant pass and then swept OVL19 for every loop bounded by 6.
items.evidence: The pass at 0x0210D6E4..0x0210D90C walks six fixed slots with add/cmp #6/blt, updating negative-status tick and DoT, positive-effect tick, +0x24 and cooldown +0x28 in that order. Nineteen loops in OVL19 are bounded by 6 and every one counts upward; none descends, sorts by speed or randomises.
items.conclusion: When two combatants become ready on the same frame, the lower slot index is serviced first. There is no priority or speed tiebreak; speed only changes when a cooldown reaches zero, through the 90 - 2*speedIndex rebuild. Recorded as BATTLE_AI_SLOT_SERVICE_ORDER.

dispatch.form: ldrb the opcode byte at pc, index a table of 8-byte C++ pointer-to-member pairs at ARM9 0x020BDEAC, blx. All 52 this-adjust words are zero, so every handler is a plain call.
dispatch.loop: The loop re-runs while flags bit 1 is set at ARM9 0x02054A08; a native clears that bit through 0x02054A24 to give the frame back.

completedBattleScriptVm.opcodeCountEvidence: The table ends at 0x020BE04C, which is where the compiler put 'script.cpp' and 'Script Stack Overflow!' for the two handlers that check the stack. Entry 52 would start inside those strings, so the last opcode is 0x33 and the count is 52. The handlers are contiguous ARM9 code, 0x02054A5C..0x0205568C, with no gaps.
completedBattleScriptVm.operandSizeEvidence: A linear decode of the whole OVL19 blob with these sizes consumes 0x021204A0..0x0212FDA4 exactly -- 23,121 instructions, ending on the byte where ARM code resumes -- and all 1,290 branch targets land on an instruction boundary. Any wrong size desynchronises the stream long before the end, so this is a proof and not a spot check.

machine.shape: A stack machine over one flat object: pc at +0x04, 96 slots at +0x08..+0x184, sp at +0x188, frameBase at +0x18C, flags at +0x190, a second array at +0x194.
machine.frames: init pushes the arguments in reverse, then a zero return address and a zero saved frame base, then sets frameBase = sp. The top frame is shaped exactly like a CALL frame, which is why RETURN stops the script when the restored pc is 0 instead of testing a depth counter.
machine.stackGuards: CALL refuses at sp >= 0x5E and CALL_NATIVE at sp >= 0x60, both asserting 'Script Stack Overflow!'. In the original the assert is only a print: execution continues and the push runs off the end of the slot array into sp and frameBase. That overrun is a defect, so the product VM raises instead of reproducing it.
machine.arithmetic: Two families. The integer set is 0x0B..0x11; the Q12 fixed-point set is 0x13..0x19. 0x15 multiplies with a +0x800 round and a 12-bit shift, 0x16 divides a value shifted left 32 and shifts the result back 20 through the NDS hardware divider at 0x04000280, and 0x18/0x19 step by 0x1000 -- those four prove the split. 0x13/0x14 and 0x23/0x25 are byte-identical to their integer counterparts, because Q12 add, subtract and shift-left are the same operation on the raw word.

blob.boundaries: 66 bytes of zero padding below the base; ARM code resumes at 0x0212FDA4
blob.entryPoints: 36 distinct addresses, from move-record fields +0x1C, +0x28 and +0x3C. All 36 are instruction boundaries and all 36 decode to a RETURN.
blob.callNative: 3,014 of the 23,121 instructions are CALL_NATIVE, naming 67 distinct OVL19 addresses between 0x0211CDFC and 0x0211EA68. None is traced.
blob.unusedOpcodes: 18 of the 52 never appear in the battle scripts, including the whole integer arithmetic family. These scripts are Q12 throughout. The unused opcodes are still implemented, because the VM belongs to the ROM and not to these scripts.

completedRngChannel.scope: The channel generator behind every battle roll: the 103-entry table, the 217-channel state, the seeder, and the exact remainder the ROM computes.
completedRngChannel.roll: ARM9 0x020431D4. roll(channel) = (seed[channel] + table[cursor[channel]]) % 103. The cursor resets to 0 on entry once it reaches 103 (cmp r1,#0x67 at 0x020431EC) and is then post-incremented. The remainder is a signed truncating one built from smull by 0x13E22CBD and asr #3, verified against C semantics across the int32 range.
completedRngChannel.seeder: ARM9 0x02043240. seed[0] = master, cursor[0] = master % 103, then for each channel 1..216 it rolls channel 0 twice: the first roll accumulates into the seed running total, the second into the cursor running total, and the channel takes seed = the seed total and cursor = the cursor total % 103.
completedRngChannel.stateIsolation: This is what closes the old residual. The header at 0x020BD230 holds the channel count 217 and the two array pointers, and those pointers occur exactly once each in the whole ARM9 image -- inside the header. Nothing but the roll and the seeder can touch the arrays, so a master seed determines the entire session and nothing can perturb it. The builder asserts this on every run.
completedRngChannel.periodicity: The roll reads the seed and never writes it, so a channel is not a stream: it is one fixed cycle of period 103. Critical hits and status procs repeat every 103 rolls on their channel. That is the original's behavior.
completedRngChannel.distributionFinding: The table is 103 entries but only 100 distinct values: 0, 50 and 99 each appear twice and 46, 100 and 102 never appear, so a roll is NOT uniform over 0..102. Over one cycle the hit count for `roll < T` is exactly T only where the shifted gaps and repeats fall above T. At the traced master seed 0x14 channel 216 is exact for every T <= 15 -- which covers the critical thresholds 2, 3, 5 and 7 -- and off by exactly one at six thresholds above it. Do not substitute a uniform generator; the skew is the original's.
masterSeedSources: ARM9 0x02000C90 -- boot, master 0, which takes the console clock at 0x0201034C. Environmental; refused rather than emulated.
ARM9 0x0206AD6C -- master loaded from a struct at +0x0C. The struct is not traced.
OVL9 0x021775DC -- `mov r0, #0x14`. A hard constant, so this reseed replays exactly.
notImplemented: The boot clock read at 0x0201034C. createChannelRng refuses a master seed of 0 rather than invent a value.
A negative cursor. The ROM's reset compare is signed, so a negative cursor would index before the table; nothing traced produces one, and the module raises instead of reading rubbish.

Nothing wires the generator into a running battle. It satisfies the rng.next(channel) interface the battle modules already take, and a test drives battleStatus with it, but no app path constructs one.

completedMatchSelection.scope: Which matches the game offers and why. This is the seam the B1 catalogs had no consumer for: the filter reads the title-event table, and OVL10 reads its payout column.

filter.rule: Walk title records 0..60 in order and keep the first `cap` whose +0x14 equals schedule slot A, whose +0x18 equals schedule slot B, and whose +0x10 is at most the progress counter shifted right by one. Return the count. The accepted value stored is the record index.
filter.scanBound: cmp ip,#0x3d at 0x02089294 -- 61 records, so index 61 is outside the scan.
filter.cap: OVL10 0x0210EC2C passes 5. In practice it never binds: the busiest schedule cell holds four.
filter.progressGate: cmp r1, r2, lsr #1 with strle at 0x02089284, where r2 is a u16 read at the session block +0xA00 +0xE8.

completedMatchSelection.scheduleGrid: ARM9 0x0207BC9C and 0x0207BCCC produce the two slots the same way: divide a clock word by a per-slot divisor in the RAM struct at 0x0210AA94 and take the remainder against a constant from 0x020C8A4C, whose first two words are 4 and 8. The data agrees decisively: across the resulting 4 x 8 grid, all 61 reachable records appear exactly once, no record in two cells and none left over. One cell, slot A 3 and slot B 4, holds no match at all.
completedMatchSelection.specialRecord: OVL10 0x0210EBFC reads a word in its own BSS; when set, the screen skips the filter and offers a list of exactly one, `mov r1, #0x3d` at 0x0210EC18 -- record 61. That word is written at exactly one address in the entire ROM, OVL10 0x0210B498, and only when the global context's +0xA8 is 4 (cmp at 0x0210B478). Two independent whole-image scans agree there is no other writer. So record 61 is the match of one entry mode, not dead data.
completedMatchSelection.payoutClosure: Not one of the 61 records the filter can offer has a zero +0x24. Record 61, the only zero in the table, is exactly the one the filter cannot reach and the one entry mode 4 forces. B1's observation and OVL8's no-reward behavior are the same fact seen from two ends.
completedMatchSelection.opponentExpansion: OVL10 0x0211057C..0x02110594 loads the team record's +0x00, +0x04 and +0x08 from three per-field bases at stride 0x14 and multiplies each by 0x44 into the preset table at 0x021105D4. That is the ROM confirming B1's corrected team base 0x020ED2D8 from the other direction. A team index of -1 and a preset slot of -1 are both 'none'.
notImplemented: What entry mode 4 is. The context field +0xA8 is compared against 4; nothing traced says what sets it.

The clock divisors at 0x0210AA94 +0x34 and +0x38. They live in RAM and nothing in the cartridge initialises them statically, so the two schedule slots are inputs to the module rather than something it computes. They are named for their offsets, not for a calendar.
The progress counter's source. The module takes it as an argument; the session block field it comes from is outside this trace.
What the screen does when the filter returns nothing -- and the grid does contain one empty cell, so that state is reachable.

completedFrameLoop.scope: The six-slot per-frame update at OVL19 0x0210D6E4: the phase order, the empty-slot skip, and the four places the loop calls out. Logic only; no screen.

loop.roster: roster[slot] is read at base + 0x5E20 + slot*4; a null entry branches straight to the loop increment, so an empty slot escapes the counters too.
loop.order: Ascending. So is every other six-bounded loop in the overlay -- all 24 of them increment, checked mechanically. Two combatants ready on the same frame therefore resolve by slot number, lowest first: that is the iteration, not a tie-break rule.

phases: 1  negative status (0x0210D700): remaining <= 0 clears and skips phase 1b; otherwise the traced tick runs and a death test follows.
1b threshold (0x0210D880), reachable only when the status code is 0: +0x22 strictly above table[stats +0x18] calls out and zeroes +0x22.
2  timer (0x0210D8B4): +0x160 non-zero gates it; +0x164 decrements while positive, else the loop calls out.
3  counters (0x0210D8DC): +0x24 then +0x28, each decrementing only while strictly positive.
completedFrameLoop.deathPath: hp < 0 after a tick stores 0 back, clears the status, sets state 0x17 and notifies 0x12, and zeroes +0x3C. Landing exactly on 0 is NOT death -- the compare is `bge`. The handler branches to phase 2 and falls through, so a combatant that dies this frame still has its timer and both counters ticked.
completedFrameLoop.thresholdTable: OVL19 0x0212FE74, u16 x 8: [100, 100, 100, 9999, 50, 9999, 50, 9999]. notImplemented: The four routines the loop calls out to: 0x0211452C on status end and on death, 0x02114984 with 0x17 and 0x02112820 with 0x12 on death, 0x0211479C when the timer runs out, and 0x021145C0 with 1 when the threshold is crossed. None is traced, so each is reported as a named event carrying its ROM address and nothing is invented for it.
The threshold index has no bound check in the original and would read into the move ladder's table; the module raises instead.

completedStateMachine.correctedHypothesis: The working guess going in was that 0x0211479C, the frame loop's timer call-out, meant 'this combatant may act'. frameFunction.order: Two six-slot loops, both ascending, both skipping an empty slot: state dispatch at 0x0210D644, then the status/threshold/timer/counter tick at 0x0210D6E4 that battleFrameLoop already models.

dispatcher.table: 0x0213040C, stride 8, the same C++ pointer-to-member form the script VM's opcode table uses. 27 states, 0x00..0x1A.
dispatcher.rule: Bit 1 of the u16 at +0x9A suspends the combatant: no handler, and the counter does not advance. Otherwise a counter at +0x16C below zero is the entry frame — it is set to 0, the handler runs, and the counter becomes 1. On later frames the handler runs only when the counter divides exactly by the state's own period at +0x170. Every non-suspended path increments.
dispatcher.periodZero: A period of 0 reaches the divide's zero path at ARM9 0x0202B750, which leaves the remainder at 0. So period 0 means every frame, not never.
dispatcher.entryCounter: 0x02114984 writes the state to +0x168 and -255 to +0x16C. Any negative would do; -255 is what the ROM writes and is kept rather than normalised.

completedStateMachine.countEvidence: Two independent bounds agree on 27. The table's 28th entry would start at 0x021304E4, where the words are 0x001F0000 and 0x01FF03E0 — neither inside OVL19's code, and UTF-16LE text follows shortly after; all 27 before it are valid OVL19 addresses. From the other side, sweeping all 70 `bl 0x02114984` sites, the literal state codes the ROM ever sets are 0, 1, 3..16 and 23.
completedStateMachine.theJoin: State 3's handler at 0x02115F38 ends at 0x021161D0 with `ldr r0,[r5,#0x28] / cmp r0,#0 / popgt`: a cooldown still running returns, and a spent one falls into state 1's routine at 0x021157BC — the negative-status action gate this repository already implements, which in turn calls AI action selection at 0x021159D4, state 2's handler. battleFrameLoop is what ticks +0x28 down. That is the whole chain from a frame to a chosen action, and all four stages were already translated.
alreadyTranslatedStates: state 2 -> 0x021159D4, battleActionSelection.selectBattleAiAction. Note it is never set by a literal `mov r1`; it is only reached from inside the machine.
state 23 -> 0x021170D0, the state battleFrameLoop's death path sets
completedStateMachine.inertStates: States 17..22 are six consecutive `bx lr` at 0x021170B8..0x021170CC. They are real table entries that do nothing, and none of the six is a code the ROM ever sets.
notImplemented: The bodies of the other twenty-one handlers. The dispatcher is traced; the module reports which handler would run rather than running one.
What bit 1 of +0x9A means, only that it suspends.
What +0x170 is initialised to at battle start. Each handler sets its own period; state 23 sets 4.
The other three frame-loop call-outs (0x0211452C is now read as the status-clear that also undoes the old code via a 0..13 jump table, but the per-code arms are not traced).

completedStateGraph.method: Each of the 27 handlers was scanned mechanically for its `mov r1,#N / bl 0x02114984` transitions, its writes to the period at +0x170, and its call targets. Two handlers were then read whole by hand; the extraction agreed with both.
completedStateGraph.shape: State 1, the action gate, is the hub and fans out to 3, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13. State 2, AI selection, fans out to 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. completedActionApplication.scope: OVL19 0x0211D71C, the script CALL_NATIVE that lands an attack. The script contract, the six-slot target walk and its four rejections, and which parameter block reaches the damage resolver. NOT the whole 2,088-byte body.
completedActionApplication.scriptContract: Three arguments. 0 is the action object, 1 is either zero or a parameter block, 2 arrives in Q12 and the entry truncates it with `asr #0xc` into the value called `kind`. The attacker is action +0xE4.
completedActionApplication.targetWalk: The same six-slot roster the frame loop walks, at base + 0x5E20 + slot*4, ascending, bounded by `cmp r0,#6` at 0x0211DF38. The routine returns the number of slots that survived every rejection.
rejections: 0x0211D79C -- the slot is the attacker itself
0x0211D7B8 -- attacker +0x54 equals target +0x54, UNLESS the attacker's status at +0x158 is exactly 5, which skips this check outright
0x0211D7EC -- the attacker's +0x94 is non-zero and the target's is zero
completedActionApplication.resolverPaths: Argument 1 of zero takes the three words at [action +0x00] + 0x28 (0x020648F0 is `add r0,r0,#4`, then +0x24) and calls the resolver at 0x0211D9E0; anything else passes argument1 + 0x24 and calls it at 0x0211D9FC. Either way the roster slot is the defender and the action object is second.
notImplemented: What `kind` selects. Only that 13 alone skips the write to action +0x20 at 0x0211DA04.
What +0x54, +0x94 and status 5 mean. All three keep their offsets as names.
The three parameter words themselves. This module locates them and hands them on; it does not interpret them.
Most of the 2,088-byte body. The action object carries its own script VM at +0x2A0 which this routine starts and steps at 0x0211DD68 and 0x0211DF04, and that nested script is not traced.

completedMoveScript.closure: B1's three unnamed pointer columns in the move table are script entry addresses, and this closes B1 -> B2 -> B4 in one line: [combatant +0x20] and [action +0x20] are the move record, +0x1C is started at OVL19 0x0211C560 on the combatant's VM at +0xEC, +0x28 at 0x0211CB7C on the same VM, and +0x3C at 0x0211C904 and 0x0211DF04 on the action's own VM at +0x2A0.
completedMoveScript.sixArgumentFrame: The +0x3C start builds `mov r2, #6`: two pointers, the action object, then three Q12 values made by `ldrsb` on move-record bytes +0x43, +0x40 and +0x41 shifted left 12, the last two added to base words. +0x40 and +0x41 are constant zero across all 596 records; +0x43 is -1 on 585 of them and 0..4 on the other eleven, so argument 3 is -1.0 in Q12 for almost every move.
completedMoveScript.argumentAddressing: A general result, provable from init alone: whatever the argument count, init argument k is local -(k+3), because init pushes the array in reverse and then two zeros. Locals -1 and -2 are those zeros. The blob agrees -- across all 23,121 instructions the negative locals used are exactly the contiguous run -3 down to -17, and nothing reads -1 or -2.
completedMoveScript.builtInScript: One path ignores the move's own column: OVL19 0x0211DD14 loads the literal 0x0212F94E and starts that with the same six-argument frame. It decodes to 161 instructions and 445 bytes -- exactly the 445-byte run B2's reachability walk could not account for, unreachable from any move record because it lives in OVL19's literal pool rather than the table. Its prologue reserves 8 locals and reads -5, -4, -3, which are arguments 2, 1 and 0.
notImplemented: The argument counts and frames for the +0x1C and +0x28 entries. Both start sites were found; neither frame was read out. A local of -17 somewhere in the blob implies an entry that passes fifteen arguments.
What arguments 0 and 1 point at, and what the two base words added to arguments 4 and 5 are.
What any of the scripts then does. That is bytecode, which battleScriptVm executes and this layer does not interpret.

completedBattleSession.scope: A screen-less session that runs the traced modules in the frame function's order and stops wherever the evidence stops, naming the seam. No UI, no invented behavior.
completedBattleSession.frameOrder: OVL19 0x0210D33C runs the state dispatch loop at 0x0210D644 and then the status/counter tick at 0x0210D6E4, both six slots ascending. The session runs both in that order.
completedBattleSession.chainThatComposes: battleFrameLoop ticks +0x28 down; state 3 returns while it is above zero and otherwise falls into state 1's routine; state 1 is battleStatus's action gate; a NORMAL family reaches AI selection. The first three links run end to end in the session and are checked by a six-slot case where every slot works through a different starting cooldown and all six reach the gate.

And a state handler must see the counter BEFORE the dispatcher's increment; the session was passing the post-increment value, so an entry frame would not have been recognised as one.

completedScriptNatives.ownerDirection: Step C of the Owner's A -> C -> B: trace the presentation natives before building the screen.
completedScriptNatives.scope: All 67 CALL_NATIVE targets catalogued mechanically; 16 of them read line by line and implemented. Those 16 carry 1,578 of the 3,014 native call sites the scripts make -- a little over half.
completedScriptNatives.catalogMethod: For each target the words up to the next target are decoded and scanned for `bl 0x02054A34` (a script argument read, with the literal index), `bl 0x02054A24` (a yield), any other `bl`, and every base-plus-displacement load or store with its width and direction. Nothing is named. The catalog's nameEvidence field says MECHANICAL_EXTRACTION_ONLY_NO_NAMES and a test asserts no entry carries a name at all.
completedScriptNatives.shape: 7,788 bytes across 67 routines, but lopsided: four are half of it and the other sixty-three average sixty bytes. By shape, 41 compound, 10 getters, 10 setters, 5 trivial, 1 yield.
implementedFindings: 0x0211CE7C / 0x0211CE94 / 0x0211CEAC -- 265, 265 and 15 calls: a chained read through +0x2C then +0x00, +0x04 or +0x08, with no null guard.
0x0211D1A8 / 0x0211D1C4 / 0x0211D1E0 -- guarded reads of +0x24, +0x28, +0x2C returning 0 for a null argument.
0x0211D2BC -- 168 calls: reads a u8 at +0x58, ADDS ONE, then shifts into Q12.
0x0211CFD8 -- reads +0x04 then +0x6DC and shifts into Q12; 0x0211CFF4 is the same chain without the shift.
0x0211CEC4 and 0x0211CEFC -- two separate routines that are both compare-and-set on +0x154: they write only when the slot is zero and return whether they did.
0x0211D514 -- 238 calls: null guard, then `asr #0xc` on argument 1 and a byte store at +0x14.
0x0211D3A8 and 0x0211D2E0 -- null guard then a tail call into a routine that was not read; the second shifts the result left by 20, not 12.
0x0211E28C -- 89 calls, 16 bytes: yield the frame and return 0.

0x0211D70C -- 56 calls, 16 bytes: `ldr ip,=0x0211D740 / mov r1,#0xd / bx ip`. A tail call into the action-application body with the kind forced to 13, which is exactly the value that routine independently treats as special. The kind-13 branch is not a mystery flag; it is this entry.
completedScriptNatives.hostBoundary: The implemented natives dereference real objects and a JavaScript rebuild has no raw addresses, so each takes a host supplying readU32/readU8/writeU32/writeU8 plus call() for the two that hand off unread routines and yield(). The offsets, the null guards and the shifts are the ROM's; the object graph is the caller's.
notImplemented: 51 of the 67. They are catalogued with their mechanical facts and calling one raises rather than returning a value nobody traced. The busiest unread ones are 0x0211D3C8 (219 calls), 0x0211D54C (214) and 0x0211E0D4 (157).
The two routines 0x0211D3A8 and 0x0211D2E0 tail-call into: ARM9 0x02047C48 and OVL19 0x0211AD9C.
What any of the 67 means. The offsets are the names.

completedCandidateBuckets.priorityCall: The Owner left the choice to this lane. The buckets were taken ahead of the remaining 51 natives because composition had shown they were the single seam stopping a battle from happening at all: every other link already ran.
completedCandidateBuckets.site: OVL19 0x02113F28, in the same function as the species move scan
completedCandidateBuckets.array: Nine groups of twelve bytes: two word entries at +0xE8 and a byte count at +0xF0. The bound is the array's own extent -- 0xE8 + 9*12 is exactly 0x154, where the next field begins, the one two of the script natives compare-and-set.
completedCandidateBuckets.fill: Two source words at stats +0x12C and +0x130. A zero is skipped. A value of 1..30 picks a group through a 31-entry jump table at 0x02113FA0; anything above 30 falls through with the group register still zero, and group 0 is never filed. So at most two entries exist across the whole array at any time, and most buckets are empty -- which is legal: the AI treats an empty list as EMPTY and falls through to the move ladder.
completedCandidateBuckets.entryMeaning: The stored value is used as a move-table index by the affordability scan at 0x02114500 (`mla r3, r0, #0x68, base`), and the same +0x12C field is used that way at 0x02111344. So an entry is an action id and its cost is the move record's +0x48. The bucket group index and the AI's state code are the same number.

A six-slot thirty-frame run produces 165 decisions across all six slots and replays identically from the same master seed.

What any bucket group number stands for. The jump table is transcribed, not interpreted.

The original writes a bucket entry with no bound check and would run past a group's two words into the next group's count. Two sources cannot reach it; this module raises rather than letting a caller reproduce the overrun.

completedActionCommit.ownerDirection: The Owner asked whether BATTLE can simply be finished. Scope stated back: a behaviourally faithful, playable battle is achievable; pixel-level presentation parity is not, because most of the original's rendering is OVL9's resource manager and the DS pipeline the web rebuild replaces. This is the first stretch of that.
completedActionCommit.finding: 0x02115924 is not state 2's tail -- it is state 1's. State 1 is the whole of gate, select and commit: it takes an action object from a pool at combatant +0x58 (0x02111F20), calls AI selection at 0x02115920, releases any previous claim when it differs, claims the new object at +0x5C, and rebuilds the cooldown.
completedActionCommit.cooldownCorrection: Reading 0x0211594C by hand gave `90 - speed*8`, from taking the magic 0x2AAAAAAB with asr #2 as a divide by 6. It is a divide by 24, so the formula is 90 - speed*2 -- which is what battleDamageResolver.baseActionCooldown already had. Verified numerically across speed 0..199 with zero mismatches rather than left on a hand reading. This is exactly the MLA/magic-number trap the brief warns about, caught by checking instead of trusting.
completedActionCommit.cooldownFacts: cooldown = 90 - 2*speed from stats +0x8C, then 80% of that when +0x160 is exactly 3. Speed 45 gives a cooldown of 0 and anything above it goes negative; since the gate is `<= 0` and the tick is `subgt`, a combatant that fast is permanently ready.
completedActionCommit.fieldUnification: +0x160 is the positive-effect code, and three modules read it three ways that now line up: the frame loop gates its timer on it being non-zero, the cooldown rebuild takes 80% when it is 3, and AI group 6 declines an action whose effect the combatant already carries. 0x0211479C clears +0x160 and +0x164 together, so the frame loop's timer is the effect's own duration.
completedActionCommit.loopClosed: With a pool supplied the session runs a self-sustaining loop with no seams at all: a combatant chooses, commits, takes a cooldown of 90-2*speed, the frame loop ticks it down, and at zero it chooses again. A six-slot run commits for every slot and replays identically from the same master seed.
notImplemented: The action pool at combatant +0x58 and its allocator at 0x02111F20. A caller supplies one; without it the commit is a named seam.
Where the AI's choice is written into the claimed object (+0x174 / +0x178 per battleActionSelection) and what reads it afterwards.
The fifteen state bodies still untraced, the 51 unread natives, and whatever ends a battle.

completedTurnStates.scope: The states a committed action passes through before it lands. States 6 and 7 and three shared predicates read whole and implemented; the shared head of 14, 15 and 16 implemented; states 4 and 5 described and deliberately not.
completedTurnStates.turnShape: 1 gate/select/commit/cooldown -> 4 or 5 (approach) or 6 or 7 (wait) -> 14, 15 or 16 (launch) -> back to 1. The mechanically extracted graph and the hand-read bodies agree on every edge.
completedTurnStates.launchSlots: Combatant +0x78, +0x7C and +0x80 hold in-flight objects. State 15 walks them at 0x02116CF8 for a zero and allocates into the first one it finds; the predicate at 0x02114464 walks the same three words and answers whether any is free. Two halves of one array read from opposite ends, and they agree: a combatant can have at most three actions in flight, and a fourth waits.
completedTurnStates.waitStates: 6 and 7 are the same routine but for one line: a free launch slot advances to 15 or 16 respectively, otherwise the combatant waits out its cooldown and re-enters the action gate to choose again. State 7 also notifies 1 on its entry frame at 0x0211648C; state 6 never does.
completedTurnStates.launchAborts: 14, 15 and 16 open identically on their entry frame and abort straight back to state 1 on either of two tests. The first differs: 14 and 15 abort when +0x17C is 8, 9, 10 or 11; 16 aborts when it is 12. All three abort on a negative +0x180. Nothing is tested after the entry frame.
predicates: 0x02114464 -- any of the three launch slots free.
0x02114490 -- +0x17C in 18..21 answers yes outright; otherwise the answer is bit 1 of +0x9A, the same suspend bit the state dispatcher reads.
0x021144B0 -- no committed action at +0x5C answers yes on its own; otherwise it defers to 0x02114490.
notImplemented: States 4 and 5, the approach geometry. 0x02116250 tests an angle against 0x4000 and 0xC000 -- the quarter and three-quarter turns of a 16-bit angle -- and offsets a target by 0x10000 before calling a DS math routine at 0x02003098. World positions and that routine are untraced, so the geometry is described and not written.
The allocator at 0x0210F8C4 and the initialiser at 0x0211C098. The second places the object at the midpoint of a box in Q12 world units, which needs the same position model.
The bodies of 14 and 16 past their shared head.
What +0x17C, +0x180 and +0x1C mean. All three keep their offsets.
completedTurnStates.launchSequence: State 15's body past the shared head, read whole: walk the three slots for a free one, allocate into it, a null allocation ends the handler with the slot left clear, a global flag at 0x02116D34 or a failed initialise at 0x0211C098 both take the identical three-line release -- clear bit 0 of the object, zero the slot, back to state 1 -- and a success aims it, raises a notify, and adds 120 to the signed halfword at +0x1C.
completedTurnStates.notifyMapping: The launch notify is the move record's own +0x10 plus eight: 0 raises 8, 1 raises 9, 2 raises 10, 3 raises 11, and anything above 3 raises nothing because the `addls` does not take. B1 catalogued that field from this exact read site; this is the mapping it produces, and since every one of the 596 records holds 0..3, every launch in the game raises one of the four.

completedLaunchPool.pool: OVL19 0x0210F8C4 scans twelve objects at globalCtx + 0x47948 + i*4 and returns the first whose first word has bit 0 clear. It walks all twelve regardless -- `cmpeq r3,#0 / moveq r3,r2` keeps the lowest free one rather than exiting early. Bit 0 is the in-use flag, and state 15's two release paths clear it with `bic r1,r1,#1`, so allocation and release are two ends of one bit.
completedLaunchPool.capacity: Twelve objects for the whole battle against three launch slots per combatant, so four of the six can exhaust the pool between them.
completedLaunchPool.whyALaunchIsRefused: The initialiser at 0x0211C098 stores the action into the new object at +0xE8 and tail-calls 0x0211C144 -- which is the action-resource charge this repository already translated. That routine refuses first on a non-zero +0x154, before it looks at cost at all, and then applies the `blt` cost gate. Both refusals return zero, and state 15 cannot tell them apart: either way it clears bit 0, zeroes the slot and goes back to state 1.
completedLaunchPool.threeWayJoin: +0x154 is one field three independent traces landed on. The two script natives at 0x0211CEC4 and 0x0211CEFC compare-and-set it. The launch charge refuses on it. And the nine-group candidate array that starts at +0xE8 ends exactly there, since 0xE8 + 9*12 is 0x154. None of the three traces was looking for the others.
notImplemented: What an in-flight object is, beyond bit 0 of its first word and the action at its +0xE8.
What +0x154 means, only that it admits one launch at a time.
The position maths in 0x0211C098, which places the object at the midpoint of a box in Q12 world units.

completedInFlight.theChain: The last link. Every frame OVL19 0x0210D694 walks all twelve pool objects and updates each one whose in-use bit is set, through 0x0211CC7C. That routine dispatches on the object's +0x04 kind, and kind 0's handler IS battleContactTargeting's walk at 0x0211C714 -- which calls the damage resolver at 0x0211C92C. So damage reaches the roster through the in-flight update, not through the state machine. No state handler ever calls the resolver, and it never needed to.
completedInFlight.frameOrderCorrection: An earlier reading of this lane said the frame function runs two loops. It runs ELEVEN, and the in-flight walk sits between the two that were named. Full list, in address order with bounds: 0x0210D3C0/6, 0x0210D490/12, 0x0210D4F8/6, 0x0210D590/6, 0x0210D624/2, 0x0210D644/6 (state dispatch), 0x0210D694/12 (in-flight update), 0x0210D6E4/6 (status and counters), 0x0210D9A8/6, 0x0210DC58/6, 0x0210DD18/2. Two of the eleven are pool walks.
completedInFlight.updateGuards: 0x0211CC7C refuses twice before dispatching: an object with no owner at +0xE4 does nothing, and an owner whose +0x94 names a different object does nothing either. Only a null lock or one naming this very object lets the update run.
completedInFlight.twoFieldsUnified: +0xE4 is the owner, and battleActionApplication reads the attacker as the action object's +0xE4 -- so an in-flight object and the 'action object' a move script operates on are one thing. +0x94 on the owner is a lock naming one in-flight object, and battleActionApplication's fourth target rejection reads the same field from the other side.
notImplemented: Kinds 1 and 2 at 0x0211CBA4 and 0x0211CC18, and the common tail at 0x0211CCE0.
The eight frame loops that are listed for their order and nothing more.
What +0x94 and the object's +0x04 kind mean beyond the dispatch they drive.

completedBattleOutcome.summary: How a match ends, who is judged to have won, and what the tournament does with it. This was the last missing link in the battle execution core: every earlier module described what happens inside a frame, and nothing described how the frames stop.
facts: Two ways a match ends: a team whose roster +0x14 reaches its +0x10 member count (end reason 2), or the frame counter at +0x5E98 passing 7200 (end reason 1). The compare is ble, so frame 7200 itself still plays.

7200 frames is 120 seconds at 60fps. The tier at +0x5E9C is min(7, frames/900). The divisor 900 was proven numerically over 0..99,999 against the magic 0x91A2B3C5 with asr #9 rather than read by hand, because that exact kind of read produced a wrong cooldown formula earlier in this lane.
The judge compares standing counts first (member +0x10 then +0x50, alive when > 0); the side with more standing wins outright. Only on a tie does it sum HP/maxHP per team.

That tie-break is IEEE-754 single precision, not Q12: 0x0202AE3C int-to-float, 0x0202A98C float divide, 0x0202A1F0 float add, 0x0202A8B0 and 0x0202A79C the two compares. Rounding at every divide and every add is modelled with Math.fround.
Verdict 4 = team 0 ahead, 3 = team 1 ahead, 5 = exactly level. 0x02110B5C demotes 5 to 3 before anything shows it.

The recorder at 0x0210E280 switches on the OVL19 static 0x0210B2DC: types 0 and 1, and every value that is not 2, win on verdict 4; type 2 wins on anything else. The demotion cannot change the flag either way, which the tests prove, so the order of the two routines does not need to be known.

The win flag is an ARRAY: session ctx +0xCAC indexed by the round cursor at +0xCA4, which advances after each round. The OVL8 payout gate requires EVERY round so far to be won, so one loss takes the whole payout. This corrects the earlier reading in battleRewardTransaction, which described +0xCAC as a single win flag.
On a win, when ctx +0xC98 is 3, a tally at +0xEAC climbs by one capped at 9999. Nothing in OVL19 clears it, so it accumulates rather than being a streak.
Slots 0..2 are team 0 and slots 3..5 are team 1: the roster init at 0x0210CAB8 indexes slot = withinTeam + base and advances base by 3 per team. Each combatant object is 0x18C bytes.

The two death tests genuinely disagree and were NOT reconciled: battleFrameLoop reports DEFEATED on hp < 0 so exactly zero survives, while the standing count here is hp <= 0. A combatant on exactly zero is alive to the frame and down to the judge.

completedInFlightSecondPass.summary: The in-flight stretch finished: kinds 1 and 2, the shared handle tail, the five script VMs per object, and two frame-ordering facts an earlier reading of this lane missed.
corrections: The frame runs TWO pool walks, not one. The first at 0x0210D490 runs only when a counter at +0x1F138 is a multiple of 8 (idiom proven numerically as x % 8) and updates only objects whose OWNER is engaged; the second at 0x0210D694 updates every in-use object. On those frames an engaged owner's object is updated twice.

The state-dispatch loop at 0x0210D644 calls 0x0210FA28 after EVERY slot and breaks out the moment anyone is engaged. The six slots do not all act on a frame where one of them commits. This was previously modelled as a plain six-slot walk.
Kinds 1 and 2 are now traced, so BATTLE_INFLIGHT_KINDS traced is [0,1,2] rather than [0]. They are not a second damage path: they step scripts.
facts: An in-flight object carries FIVE script VMs: one at +0xEC and four in an array at +0x2A0 with stride 0x1B4. Kind 1 steps all five; kind 2 steps only the four and reports whether any stayed active. Active is bit 0 of a VM's +0x190.

When a VM goes inactive, 0x0211CD80 releases what it held: three parallel 24-entry arrays on the object, the handle at +0x24, its owning script at +0x84, a binding at +0x970, with the handle's byte +0x5B cleared and any binding naming it unbound. The shared tail at 0x0211CCE0 walks the same twenty-four.
0x0210FA28 is the is-any-of-the-six-engaged test, reading the same +0x94 lock the in-flight update and battleActionApplication read. Engaged and holding an in-flight object are one statement.
All eleven frame loops now carry their call targets. Seven remain untranslated and are recorded as addresses plus callees only: a call target is not a meaning.

completedSessionClosure.summary: battleSession now runs a battle to a verdict instead of to a caller-supplied bound. The frame is dispatch with the engagement break, then status and counters, then the clock, then the end check, judge and demotion.
facts: runBattleSession stops on the traced end conditions and reports reason and verdict; the old comment saying the states that end a battle were not traced is retired.

The end check is applied only when both teams have at least one member. The ROM wipe compare is downed >= count and its rosters always have three a side, so count == 0 is outside the domain of that compare; answering 0 >= 0 as a wipe would be answering a question the ROM never asks.

completedCreatureBuild.summary: Where a combatant's stats come from. Until this, a battle could only run on made-up inputs.
facts: The preset-to-creature mapping was derived by emulating the decoded instruction stream, not read by eye. A scratchpad emulator printed every creature offset and what reached it.

A creature is a species id plus ten small level numbers. Every stat is curve[level]; nothing is computed. HP takes its level from the SPECIES record +0x30, the other nine from the PRESET +0x14..+0x38.

The curve is 27 rows of eight u16 at 0x020CA008. Column 0 is HP, 200 to 7000. Columns 1 through 6 are byte-identical, which is why the compiler could share one base register and why sharing a column changes no value. Column 7 runs 4 to 20 and the builder never reads it.
This is the same stride-16 table the very first handoff review verified as EXACT_MATCH without knowing its purpose.
The species table is 228 records of 0x84 and 228 is also the absent marker, so the marker is one past the last id rather than a magic number.

One preset carries -1 in a level field, which would read in front of the curve. It never happens: that record names the absent species and is skipped before any level is read. Recorded as a thing not to clamp.

combatant+0x10 IS the creature record, so the judge reading member+0x10+0x50 is reading the creature's HP. The move list is built by scanning all 596 move records for ones whose +0x00 matches the species, capped at eight.

completedDamageWiring.summary: The in-flight phase is composed into the frame and damage flows; a live match does not yet deal any, for a traced reason.
facts: battleDamageCore's BATTLE_STAT_CURVE is column 1 of the 27-row creature curve catalogued today. Same table, proven by assertion rather than assumed.
attackerIndex is the attacker creature's +0x84, raised one step when its +0x160 or +0x158 is exactly 1.

defenderIndex is chosen by the action record's +0x58 from six creature levels: +0x88 (selector 0 and anything above 5), +0x94, +0x98, +0x9C, +0xA0, +0xA4, each raised by its own buff code 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 7.
The in-flight phase sits between the dispatch loop and the tick loop, which is where BATTLE_FRAME_LOOPS already put 0x0210D694.
A session given a contact resolver drives six slots to real damage with no seam left; without one the phase is a named seam.
completedDamageWiring.blocker: selectBattleAiAction reads its three buckets from combatant +0xE4/+0xE5/+0xE6, written by the creature loader at OVL19 0x02113D88 as it classifies the moves it scanned for the species. The session passes buildCandidateBuckets' nine groups instead, which live at +0xE8 + group*12 and feed the targeted cascade. Next read: the classification at 0x02113E60..0x02113F08.

completedDamageWiring.correction: The contact walk is not where an ordinary attack resolves. Kinds 0 and 1, which hold every real power from 30 to 600, reach the resolver from the script native 0x0211D71C; the walk handles only kinds 2 and 3, whose powers are 0 or 15. The runtime resolveContact therefore sits on the smaller of the two paths, which is why a live match still shows no HP loss.

completedAiComposition.summary: The AI ladder now has candidates and a reserve, and commits real damage-route moves.
facts: The reserve scalar is the battle clock tier at ctx +0x5E9C, read at 0x021159F0 and indexing 0x0212FFF4 stride 16. Percents ramp 0,40,50,60,70,80,90,100 for profile 0.
The ladder buckets come from the creature move list classified at 0x02113E5C by the move record +0x50, with kind 1 split on +0x0C. Three per bucket.
Bucket 4 has no cost gate, so a free kind-0 move is available at tier 0 while the reserve is still zero.
The bucketed kinds 0 and 1 are exactly the kinds the resolver routes to the curve-and-power term; kinds 2 and 3, which the contact walk handles, are never bucketed.

openBattleScriptDecision.summary: Executing the original move scripts requires carrying the OVL19 script segment in the product.
openBattleScriptDecision.proven: The VM runs the real bytecode and dispatches real natives; 15, 6 and 20 distinct natives from a single move record three pointers.
theTwoOptions: Carry the segment. The VM then runs the original scripts and move behaviour is not reimplemented at all, which is the most faithful option available. Cost: about 86 KB of cartridge bytecode lives in the product tree, which the firewall payload test would not catch but its title covers.
Do not carry it. Move behaviour then has to be written by hand across 22,032 instructions of reachable script, which is exactly what rule 1 forbids guessing at.
openBattleScriptDecision.recommendation: Carry it. The project premise is faithfulness, the VM is already traced and tested, and the alternative is inventing behaviour at a scale rule 1 exists to prevent. But it changes what ships, so it is the Owner call.
openBattleScriptDecision.nextIfCarried: Model the action object the scripts read. They currently run on zeros, so their branches go the wrong way and none reaches 0x0211D71C.
openBattleScriptDecision.resolution: The Owner authorized carrying the segment on 2026-09-02. It was already in battle-scripts.r1.json from the B2 pass, byte identical; the duplicate written today was deleted. The firewall now names the one authorized segment.

completedMoveScriptRun.summary: A real move record executes the cartridge own script on the traced VM.

The launch at 0x0211C198 rewrites two pointers in place before starting them, and the second test reads the first store, so one record can take both.
The +0x3C column runs on the VM array at +0x2A0 with the six-argument frame battleMoveScript traced; +0x1C and +0x28 run on +0xEC.
A kind-1 move of power 400 dispatches 20 distinct natives.
The yield at 0x0211E28C was the blocker, not the decode. With natives routed, a real attack script executes 280 instructions and ends cleanly.
Native coverage is 18 of 67 routines over 2,011 of 3,014 call sites.
Sweeping every distinct script address: 36 run, 9 clean, 27 stop on an unread native, 1 reaches 0x0211D71C.

completedDamageChain.summary: A live match runs on cartridge data only, deals damage, knocks a side down and returns a verdict.
completedDamageChain.observed: Two seeds: 181 and 271 frames, both TEAM_DOWN with TEAM_ZERO_AHEAD. Player 1080 down to 929 and 992, opponent 520 down to 0 and marked down. rosterEvidence VERIFIED_BINARY.
facts: The attack runs on the +0x28 column, which reaches 0x0211D71C, holds 31 distinct scripts against two for +0x3C, and is the one the launch initialiser rewrites.
0x0211D71C is nine instructions that read the kind out of Q12 and tail into 0x0211D740, the body 0x0211D70C enters with the kind forced to 13.

The script VM was rebuilt every frame, so a script restarted from the top and fired once per frame instead of once. It now persists per action.
Combatants started in state 1 rather than the cooldown gate, so every one committed on every frame and a match was over in three.

completedDefeatedState.summary: State 0x17 has a translated body, and the two call-outs the death path makes are applied rather than only announced. The seam a composed session reported for state 23 is closed.
completedDefeatedState.tableRedumped: The 27-entry dispatch table at 0x0213040C was read from the ROM again rather than taken from this file: index 0x17 is 0x021170D0, and the 28th entry is 0x001F0000, outside OVL19. Both agree with the earlier reading.

body.shape: Thirteen instructions. Entry frame (+0x16C == 0): arm +0x170 to 4 and return. Otherwise read +0x17C: any value but 1 re-arms 4 and returns; exactly 1 falls into state 1's routine at 0x021157BC with the same combatant.
body.threeNegatives: It never calls 0x02114984, so nothing in this handler moves a combatant out of 0x17 -- being down is durable. It applies no HP test, and 0x021157BC opens straight onto the +0x158 jump table with no liveness gate of its own, so a defeated combatant on the code-1 arm really does run the action gate. And the falling-through arm does not rewrite the period, so the 4 armed on the entry frame stands.

theGateField.finding: +0x17C is the notify code a combatant was last given. That is what state 0x17 tests.
theGateField.traced: 0x02112928 reads the code the combatant is ALREADY carrying and indexes a 26-entry pointer-to-member table built on the stack from a template at 0x0211F7D0; a null entry skips the call. Then 0x02112964 stores the new code to +0x17C and 0x0211296C arms +0x180 at -255. There is exactly one exit, so both stores always happen.
theGateField.notTraced: The 26 exit routines. The table is assembled on the stack and this lane has not walked it, so the code whose routine would have run is named on the event and nothing is invented for it.
theGateField.everyWriter: A whole-overlay scan for immediate-offset accesses at +0x17C finds 30, of which seven are stores. Four of the seven are on a different structure (base r4+0x19000). The three on a combatant are 0x02112964 (this notify), 0x02114124 (the initialiser at 0x021140D0, which writes 0 to both +0x168 and +0x17C at battle start) and 0x02117278 (a block zeroing).

completedDefeatedState.defectFoundByRunningIt: 0x02114984 is four instructions and writes BOTH +0x168 and +0x16C -- `mvn r1,#0xfe` is -255. The death path was setting only the state. A probe over twelve frames showed a defeated combatant with its counter still climbing out of state 3 (1, 2, 3 ...) and the period stuck at state 3's 1, so the dispatcher never gave state 0x17 an entry frame and it never armed its own period of 4. After the fix the same probe reads counter -255 on the death frame, then period 4 from the entry frame on.
completedDefeatedState.secondGap: runStatusWaitState returned a notify code from the day it was written and the session dropped it, so +0x17C never moved. It is applied now, which is what makes state 23's gate reachable at all.
completedDefeatedState.measuredBeforeAndAfter: seed 0x14: 181 frames, TEAM_DOWN, TEAM_ZERO_AHEAD, hp [1080,1080,-,520] -> [929,992,-,0]. seed 0x20: 271 frames, same verdict, hp -> [874,961,-,0]. Identical before and after, which is the expected result: the fix changes what a combatant does AFTER it is down.
completedDefeatedState.whatARealMatchShows: Every one of the currently reachable matches ends on the very frame of its first death, because each opponent team expands to a single member and the first death is therefore a wipe. Twelve player-team indices were run: firstDown equals the last frame in every match that ends on a wipe. So state 0x17 is entered on the final frame and never dispatched in a runtime match today. The seam it raised was reachable in composed sessions, and there it went from 11 in 12 frames to 0.

What any notify code means beyond the number. Codes seen so far: 1, 0x12, and the 8..12 and 18..21 ranges battleTurnStates already reads.
The other twenty-four handler bodies.

completedDeepScriptFrame.supersedes: The recorded item 'one script entry has not been found; the blob reads a local implying fifteen arguments and the widest traced frame is fourteen'.
completedDeepScriptFrame.summary: There is no missing start site. A script-level CALL builds its own frame, so a fifteen-deep frame never had to come from an init.
completedDeepScriptFrame.theMechanism: ARM9 0x02055500, the CALL handler, does what the init does: 0x02055538 pushes the return address (pc + 5), 0x02055554 pushes the caller's frame base, 0x0205555C sets the frame base to the new depth. A callee's locals -1 and -2 are those two words -- the slots init fills with zeros -- and -3 downward reach whatever the caller left on the stack. The addressing rule is identical; only the order differs, because init reverses the argument array and a CALL does not.
completedDeepScriptFrame.whereTheMinus17Is: All three uses of local -17 in the blob are in one routine, 0x02128680. It is not in the move table and is reached only by two CALLs, at 0x021292EA and 0x02129319. Both callers are +0x28 entries, so both hold fourteen arguments of their own: record 565 (species 215) at 0x021292C9 pushes the literal 0x00001000, Q12 1.0, and record 441 (species 176) at 0x021292F8 pushes 0x00000000; each then pushes its own fourteen from local -16 down to -3. Pushing them high-to-low undoes init's reversal, so inside 0x02128680 locals -3..-16 mean exactly what they meant in the caller and -17 is the prepended literal.
completedDeepScriptFrame.theRomCountsItToo: Both call sites are followed by POP.N 0x8F. The operand is an UNSIGNED byte -- ARM9 0x02054BF8 is `ldrb`, and bit 7 is a slide flag, not a sign -- so the low seven bits are 15. The frame depth is counted by the cartridge, not inferred here. An earlier signed reading of this operand would have printed -113.
completedDeepScriptFrame.checkedFromTheOtherSide: Every ARM-mode BL to the init at 0x020548D4, across ARM9 and all 22 overlays, is one of 24 sites. The argument counts they pass are only 0, 1, 6, 8 and 14. Nothing in the image passes fifteen.
completedDeepScriptFrame.newFactAlongTheWay: The +0x1C entry passes 8 arguments (`mov r2,#8` at 0x0211C51C), which this file previously listed as untraced. The +0x28 entry passes 14 (`mov r2,#0xE` at 0x0211CABC, array at sp+0, stores running sp+0x00..sp+0x34). Sixteen of the 24 init sites pass 0 with a null script address, which is the VM being cleared rather than started.

completedSpriteCellBox.twoOfThoseThreeWordsWereWrong: It is not one routine, it is three calls deep. And the arithmetic at the end of it needs nothing from the art: it is now translated whole, with the resource left as the only input.
completedSpriteCellBox.theChain: ARM9 0x02047E58: [obj+0xC8] -> 0x02049714 (ldr r0,[r0,#4], two instructions) -> 0x02048B98 (ldr r0,[r0], two instructions) -> 0x0202DD54 with the halfword at [[obj+0x70]] as the index.
completedSpriteCellBox.bankLookup: 0x0202DD54 is a bounds-checked indexed read over a header of {u16 count, u16 attribute, u32 arrayBase}. The compare is UNSIGNED (cmp r1,r2 / movhs r0,#0), so an out-of-range index returns null and a negative one does not read backwards. Attribute bit 0 selects a stride of 16, otherwise 8. Derived check: the box is at +0x8..+0xE, so it only fits the 16-byte stride.
completedSpriteCellBox.whichHalfwordIsWhich: Taken from the ROM's own rounding rather than from a sprite-format write-up. In the scale pass one edge of each pair is computed with mla against -4095 and the other with mul then +4095, both then asr #12 -- rounding one edge down and the other up is what a bounding box does. So +0x0C is the low X edge and +0x08 the high, +0x0E the low Y and +0x0A the high; the object's copies are +0xD0/+0xCC and +0xD2/+0xCE.
completedSpriteCellBox.theTransform: r1 == 0, or no flip with both scales exactly 0x1000, returns the cell's own box at cell+8 (0x02047FF0). Otherwise +0x14 bit 0 flips X and bit 1 flips Y -- negate the pair and swap it, so the low edge stays low -- then the Q12 scales at +0x04 and +0x08 are applied, a negative scale swapping which edge feeds which. Every store is a strh, so every result truncates to a signed halfword. The identity check skips the rounding as well, so 0x1000 is not the same as multiplying by one.
completedSpriteCellBox.verifiedNumerically: The ARM was transcribed instruction by instruction into a scratch script and 4,000 randomised inputs were run through both it and the module: 0 mismatches. Thirty-seven of those vectors, one per combination of flip bits and scale signs, are embedded in the test so the check survives the scratch script.
completedSpriteCellBox.howNarrowTheGapNowIs: The launch initialiser passes r1 = 1 unconditionally (0x0211C0C0), so a launch never takes the r1 == 0 exit. Its fourth argument comes from fields this lane already holds: the committed action at +0x5C (0x02116B70, 0x02116D70), the target at +0x64 (0x02116F3C), and the return of 0x02112394 at 0x0211716C. The sprite object is that thing's +4. What is left outside is one field on an object the battle lane already carries, not the box.
completedSpriteCellBox.whyTheDumpWasNotDone: Walking [X+4]'s +0xC8 into a loaded resource is the OVL9 resource manager's and the art lane's. A table of original boxes dumped now would have nothing to align to, because the remake's own art is not generated. The routine that consumes such a table is in place, so the dump can happen the moment the art does.

completedAnimationNatives.correctionToTheGrouping: This file and the handoff called all three animation natives supplied by the cell box. Only two of the three touch it. 0x0211D238 calls 0x02047E58 with r1 = 1 and 0x0211D298 calls 0x02047D98, which does its own walk; 0x0211D33C calls 0x02047E00, which reads the animation table at [obj+0x8C] and never looks at a cell at all.

bodies.0x0211D238: The cell box's Y midpoint in Q12. Reads the returned pointer at +6 (low Y) and +2 (high Y), adds them, shifts left 12, THEN halves toward zero with `add r0,r0,r0,lsr #31 / asr r0,r0,#1`. The order matters: an odd sum keeps its half unit, which halving first would have discarded.
bodies.0x0211D298: The cell box's Y extent in Q12, via 0x02047D98: the same walk, then `ldrsh [+0xA] - ldrsh [+0xE]`. No transform is applied, so this is the record's own height and not the object's scaled copy.
bodies.0x0211D33C: The animation table's summed u16 at +4, in Q12, via 0x02047E00: count at [[obj+0x8C]], array base at +0xC read once, entries of eight bytes. An empty table returns 0 -- the compare is `cmp ip,#0 / bxls lr`, unsigned.

completedAnimationNatives.theAccessorFamily: 0x02047D98 (Y extent), 0x02047DCC (X extent), 0x02047E00 (the table sum) and 0x02047E38 (one entry, indexed through 0x0202E364) sit immediately below 0x02047E58 and share its walk.
completedAnimationNatives.secondIndependentProofOfTheEdgeRoles: 0x02047DCC computes `[+0x8] - [+0xC]` and 0x02047D98 computes `[+0xA] - [+0xE]`. An extent is high minus low, so +0x08 and +0x0A are the high edges and +0x0C and +0x0E the low ones. That is the same answer the scale pass's rounding directions gave, reached from a different routine -- the earlier reading is confirmed rather than merely restated.
completedAnimationNatives.whatTheSummedFieldMeans: UNKNOWN_REQUIRES_TRACE. It is summed over every entry and shifted into Q12, which is what a total duration would look like, but the field has not been read from the other side, so it keeps its offset for a name.
